y0: Humble and Riding on a Donkey
y1: Just before the Passover, Jerusalem was full of pilgrims. Jesus intentionally had a donkey prepared. Matthew quotes: “Tell the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’”
y2: The crowd sings: “Hosanna to the Son of David.” But the people of the city ask, “Who is this?” and the crowd answers, “This is the prophet, Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” They still didn't fully know who He was.
y3: A king who won a war would ride a warhorse into the city. A donkey is the mount of a king of peace ( with Solomon). continues: “He will cut off the chariot... and the battle bow will be cut off; and he will speak peace to the nations.” The crowd expected a king who would drive out Rome, but Jesus was a different kind of King.
y5: The Court of the Gentiles was the only place where foreigners could also pray to God. But it was full of people selling sacrificial animals and money changers. Because the temple tax could only be paid with a special Tyrian silver coin, they charged exchange fees.
y6: Jesus quotes (“My house shall be called a house of prayer”) and (“a den of robbers”) together. A den of robbers isn't where the robbery happens, but where the robbers hide. It is an accusation that the temple had become a place hiding injustice behind religious rituals.
y7: Jesus' anger is not for Himself, but for God's house and for the foreigners and the poor who were being pushed out of it. In the very next verse, Jesus heals the blind and the lame in that same temple. After overturning it, He restores it.
y9: According to tradition, it was difficult for the blind and the lame to enter deep into the temple (). But Jesus heals them right inside that temple. The temple returned to its true purpose.
y10: The children shouted the song they had learned on the road inside the temple. The chief priests were furious, but Jesus quotes: “Out of the mouth of children and nursing babies you have perfected praise.” The religious leaders didn't see it, but the children did.
y11: “I thank you... that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.” The prayer from chapter 11 came true exactly like this in the temple.
y13: When a fig tree sprouts leaves, it also begins to produce small early fruits (page). A tree with abundant leaves but no fruit is in a state of “looking like it has something, but having nothing.” At Jesus' word, the tree withered at once.
y14: This action is an “acted parable” that explains the previous temple scene. A temple with grand worship and many sacrifices, but without the fruit God is looking for (justice, mercy, prayer). Then Jesus teaches His disciples about praying with unwavering faith.
y15: Jesus wasn't just taking out His anger. Old Testament prophets (;) compared Israel to a fruitless fig tree. Jesus was prophesying with an action instead of words. The warning applies to us as well.
verse: “Tell the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’”
prayer: Jesus, the humble King who came riding on a donkey, hosanna! Please rule over me not according to my expectations, but in Your way. Cleanse my heart to be a house of prayer, and help me to bear the fruit of justice and mercy, rather than having a faith with only leaves. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: donkey. David's son Solomon was also made king while riding a donkey (). It represents humility and peace, not military power. Only Matthew mentions both the donkey and its colt, accurately showing Zechariah's prophecy.
d1: hosanna. It is a prayer from. Pilgrims used to sing this song as they went up to the temple. Ironically, Jesus is indeed going to the cross to save “now.”
d2: praise. It is a quote from (Septuagint). Through the mouths of weak children, God silences His enemies. Jesus defended the children's praise by quoting Scripture.
d3: fig tree. Along with the grapevine, it is a tree that symbolizes Israel. It was supposed to show its faithfulness through fruit. There is also a parable of the fig tree in.
